# generator-shortcuts

## Assigned question

Find the strongest plausible shortcut or rival rule that fits the canonical demonstrations. Give an exact input on which it disagrees with the intended rule, how the output was checked, and whether the generator emits such cases.

## Answer

There is not just one canonical-fitting shortcut. The final review names six executable rules that reproduce all 3/3 public pairs:

1. `first_marker_per_code` — infer the stencil and transforms correctly, but stamp only the first occurrence of each marker color;
2. `template_only_in_left_strip` — search for stencil colors only in columns 0–4;
3. `first_five_template_cells` — ignore every source cell after the first five in reading order;
4. `ignore_color_one` — treat color `1` as absent from the stencil;
5. `canonical_template_boxes_only` — run the correct rule only for source boxes `3×2` or `3×3`; and
6. `canonical_grid_sizes_only` — run the correct rule only for grids `12×19`, `13×19`, or `13×20`.

The first rule is the strongest semantic shortcut: it understands nearly the entire task but misses repeated same-code anchors, a feature absent from every public pair. The two size-gated rules created the widest measured curriculum hole in version `3.1.0`: each fit 35/210 three-demo windows per band and failed every corresponding query.

## How the claims were checked

1. Each of the six callables was run on every canonical input and compared to the canonical output. All six matched 3/3.
2. The intended Python mirror and each rival were run on generated inputs and compared cell-by-cell. The v2 probe records full outputs, hashes, and the first differing cell.
3. The official Racket-backed semantic gate independently verified all 10/10 rival claims on generated witnesses and accepted 600/600 strict inputs.
4. The official after battery passed rule smoke, authority sync, and all ten other stages; the selected Racket authority was not changed.
5. Every cyclic three-demo start in the full 210-step schedule was evaluated in easy, medium, and hard. After the repair, each of all ten lesson competitors disagrees with at least one visible demonstration in all 630 windows.

## Did the old generator emit discriminators?

Partially, but not reliably at lesson level.

Version `3.1.0` emitted individual counterexamples for all four second-round rivals, yet its profile order and random feature placement allowed ambiguous three-demo windows. The exact pre-fix counts were:

| Rival | Easy survivors / query failures | Medium | Hard |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| canonical template boxes only | 35 / 35 | 35 / 35 | 35 / 35 |
| canonical grid sizes only | 35 / 35 | 35 / 35 | 35 / 35 |
| first five template cells | 17 / 9 | 16 / 8 | 20 / 13 |
| ignore color `1` | 1 / 1 | 1 / 1 | 1 / 1 |

That distinction matters: having counterexamples somewhere in the distribution is insufficient when the training unit is a three-demo lesson.

## Does the repaired generator emit them reliably?

Yes, for the declared default lesson policy. Version `3.2.0` alternates canonical and expanded dimension profiles and places a feature-expanding example in every period-3 block. The final retained probe reports:

- zero survivor starts for every one of ten lesson rivals in easy, medium, and hard;
- zero starts missing a noncanonical grid size;
- zero starts missing a noncanonical template box;
- zero starts missing a stencil with more than five cells; and
- zero starts missing color `1`.

The guarantee applies to consecutive default schedule windows. A downstream system that assembles lessons from arbitrary nonconsecutive indices should rerun the retained probe against that assembly policy.
